lead: This unit shows how IoT ideas become working systems in homes, cities, factories, vehicles, health care and water supply. After it you can read a use case, choose the sensors and network, size the data and power, and explain the deployment choices for each domain.
about: Chapter 6.1 starts with the home, where sensors, a hub and simple rules switch lights and send alerts. Chapter 6.2 scales the same chain to city parking over NB-IoT. Chapter 6.3 moves into factories and the Industry 4.0 automation hierarchy. Chapter 6.4 explains the feedback loop shared by drones, robots and automotive systems such as ABS and adaptive cruise control. Chapter 6.5 applies remote monitoring to health and water. Chapter 6.6 compares domain case studies in agriculture, retail, logistics, energy and environment, and shows how to size data, choose a network and state deployment limits.

chapters.idea: A smart home turns sensor events into local or cloud rules that switch actuators and inform the user.
chapters.depth: Cover the home as a small IoT system: sensors (PIR, door, temperature), actuators (relay, smart plug, siren), a home hub or gateway, local rules and cloud rules. Compare local control that survives a power cut with cloud control that works from outside. Include home infrastructure security at the level of door and camera alerts. Show a Raspberry Pi or Arduino as a web-enabled constrained device that serves a small page and reads a sensor. Some syllabi call this evaluating a home automation system. Keep MQTT packet details for Unit 3.

figure.title: Smart home control path
figure.aria: A home hub collects motion and door events and can send them to cloud rules that switch a relay lamp and notify a phone app.

chapters.example: A home has 10 smart bulbs rated 9 W used 5 h a day, one hub rated 3 W running all day, and 2 cameras rated 5 W running all day. Electricity costs ₹7.50 per kWh. Find the monthly energy use and cost for 30 days. Bulbs: 10×9 W×5 h=450 Wh/day. Hub: 3 W×24 h=72 Wh/day. Cameras: 2×5 W×24 h=240 Wh/day. Total=762 Wh/day=0.762 kWh/day. For 30 days: 22.86 kWh. Cost=22.86×7.50=₹171.45.
chapters.trap: Do not treat standby power as zero; standby loads run 24 h and often dominate. Keep W and kW consistent: divide Wh by 1000 before multiplying by the tariff.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 sensors and actuators; Unit 3 MQTT basics; Unit 4 Arduino or Raspberry Pi interfacing; Unit 5 cloud basics.
chapters.leave: MQTT packet format and security to Unit 3 and Unit 5; relay driver circuits to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A smart city uses many small sensing deployments, and smart parking shows the full chain from sensor to payment over a low-power wide-area network.
chapters.depth: Cover smart city services (mobility, lighting, waste, water) and then smart parking in detail: in-ground or overhead slot sensors, gate or barrier, driver app, payment. Explain NB-IoT devices, NB-IoT baseline deployment, mobile operator deployment and simulation of NB-IoT networks at the level of what is deployed and why. Include vehicle management with network selection: pick 4G, NB-IoT or Wi-Fi by data rate, latency, power and cost. Refer to MQTT as the message path. Some syllabi call this the smart parking use case.

figure.title: Smart parking message path
figure.aria: A parking slot sensor sends small NB-IoT messages through the operator core to a parking cloud that updates a driver app and payment.

chapters.example: A car park has 200 slots. Each slot sensor sends one 60-byte message every 5 minutes. Find the average uplink bit rate and the data volume per day. Messages: 200×12=2400 per hour=0.6667 per second. Rate=0.6667×60 B=40 B/s=320 bit/s. Daily messages: 200×12×24=57,600. Data: 57,600×60 B=3,456,000 B=3.456 MB/day.
chapters.trap: NB-IoT is for small, infrequent uplink. Do not use it for live video from the barrier camera. Convert messages per hour to per second before finding bit rate.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 LPWAN, NB-IoT and MQTT; Unit 5 cloud services.
chapters.leave: NB-IoT physical layer and attach signalling to Unit 3; payment security to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: IIoT connects machines and business systems so that production data drives control, maintenance and planning across the plant.
chapters.depth: Cover Industry 4.0 as cyber-physical production: digital twin, smart factory, predictive maintenance, big data and visualization. Teach the automation hierarchy from sensor and actuator to PLC, SCADA, MES and ERP. Include sensor nodes on machines, edge versus cloud, and OEE as the plant metric. Mention OPC-UA and SCADA only as integration names; their protocol details are in Unit 3. Keep the security lifecycle at the level of update policy and access control; Unit 5 owns the mechanisms. Some syllabi call this industrial automation.

figure.aria: The industrial automation hierarchy from field sensors and PLCs up through SCADA and MES to ERP.

chapters.example: A machine is scheduled for 480 min. It is down for 48 min. It makes 800 parts; 760 are good. Ideal cycle time is 30 s per part. Find availability, performance, quality and OEE. Run time=480−48=432 min. Availability=432/480=0.900. Performance=(0.5 min×800)/432=0.926. Quality=760/800=0.950. OEE=0.900×0.926×0.950=0.792=79.2%.
chapters.trap: Performance uses total count, not good count; quality is applied separately. Convert ideal cycle time to the same unit as run time, here minutes.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 sensors and sensor nodes; Unit 3 industrial protocols; Unit 5 data analytics.
chapters.leave: PLC programming and SCADA details to Unit 3; machine-learning algorithms to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A cyber-physical system joins computation and a physical process in a closed feedback loop, so timing and sensing errors change the physical result.
chapters.depth: Cover cyber-physical systems as computation plus a physical process in a closed loop. Use mechatronics examples: electronic ignition, ABS, EBD, adaptive cruise control, drone actuation and control, an autonomous robot with a vision system, and a robotic camera dolly. Explain sampling period, actuator delay and sensor error in each. Only a few universities teach the drone control equations; keep those at block level. Some syllabi call this mechatronics and IoT case studies.

figure.title: CPS feedback loop
figure.aria: A cyber-physical system measures a physical process, computes a command and drives actuators that change the process, closing the loop.

chapters.example: A wheel has radius 0.32 m and a 48-tooth tone ring. The car moves at 60 km/h. Find the wheel angular speed and the pulse frequency from the ABS sensor. Speed=60/3.6=16.67 m/s. Angular speed ω=v/r=16.67/0.32=52.08 rad/s. Revolutions per second=52.08/(2π)=8.29. Pulse frequency=8.29×48=397.9 Hz.
chapters.trap: Do not use km/h directly with radius in metres. Convert to m/s. The tone-ring frequency is per wheel revolution, not per second of vehicle travel.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 sensors and actuators; Unit 4 interfacing; Unit 3 industrial protocols for plant examples.
chapters.leave: PID tuning and control theory to a control systems course; wireless protocol details to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Remote monitoring puts a sensor, a gateway and a cloud service between a distant process and the person who acts, with alarms when limits are crossed.
chapters.depth: Cover remote monitoring systems and remotely operated autonomous systems. For e-health: wearables, ECG, SpO2, fall detection and alert escalation. For water: centralized water management with tank level, pump control, leak detection and a water-level control lab. Include data rate, battery life and alarm thresholds. Some syllabi call this remote monitoring systems. Keep medical certification and pump hydraulics out. Cloud lab tasks such as creating a VM or allocating CPU and memory belong with Unit 5; use them only to host the dashboard.

figure.aria: A sensor reading travels every minute through a gateway and cloud, where a threshold check sends an alert to a remote operator or clinician.

chapters.example: A tank is 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and 1.2 m deep. A 0.5 HP pump fills it at 20 L/min. Find the volume, the fill time and the energy cost at ₹7 per kWh. Volume=2×1.5×1.2=3.6 m³=3600 L. Fill time=3600/20=180 min=3 h. Pump electrical power=0.5×746=373 W=0.373 kW. Energy=0.373×3=1.119 kWh. Cost=1.119×7=₹7.83.
chapters.trap: 1 HP is about 746 W, not 1000 W. 1 m³ is 1000 L. Keep the pump hydraulic power separate from electrical input power; this example uses electrical power.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 sensors; Unit 3 MQTT; Unit 4 Raspberry Pi; Unit 5 cloud dashboards.
chapters.leave: Medical device certification and hospital IT to a biomedical course; pump hydraulics to fluid mechanics.

chapters.idea: The same IoT building blocks take different shapes in agriculture, retail, logistics, energy and environment, and a case study is judged by its constraints, not by the sensor list.
chapters.depth: Cover domain-specific IoT in agriculture (soil moisture, portable wireless interactive sensors), retail, logistics, energy, environment, wearables and vehicle management with network selection. Teach a case-study method: problem, sensors, network, data rate, power, cost and failure mode. Use big data and visualization to compare sites. Security topics such as authentication, privacy-preserving aggregation and informed consent appear only as deployment constraints; Unit 5 owns the protocols. Some syllabi call this domain-specific IoTs.
chapters.example: A farm uses 500 soil-moisture sensors. Each sends an 80-byte message every 10 minutes. Find the messages per day and the data volume per day. If the LoRaWAN payload limit is 51 bytes, what must change? Messages per sensor per day=24×6=144. Total=500×144=72,000 messages/day. Data=72,000×80 B=5,760,000 B=5.76 MB/day. 80 B is above 51 B, so the reading must be split, compressed or sent over a larger-payload link such as NB-IoT.
chapters.trap: Do not size a network from sensor count alone; use message size and interval. A 51-byte payload limit cannot carry an 80-byte reading in one frame without fragmentation or compression.
chapters.prereq: All earlier chapters, especially Unit 3 protocols and Unit 5 analytics and security.
chapters.leave: Detailed security protocols to Unit 5; business model economics to Unit 1.
